title: Upgrade to MCP v2 (spec 2026-07-28)
body:
## Summary

Upgrade Homarr's MCP server from the current 2025 Streamable HTTP implementation to the new **MCP v2** specification ([2026-07-28](https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28)). MCP v2 is a major rewrite that makes the protocol **fully stateless**, simplifies deployment, and adds several production-grade improvements.

## Why MCP v2 is better

### 1. Stateless protocol (the big one)

The old protocol required a stateful `initialize`/`initialized` handshake, an `Mcp-Session-Id` header, and sticky sessions. This forced servers to manage session state, drain/migrate active sessions on deploy, and reconnect on instance loss. **MCP v2 removes the handshake, the session header, and protocol sessions from the request path entirely.** Each request carries its own protocol version, client identity, and capabilities. A server can now run as a plain stateless HTTP workload — ideal for Homarr's self-hosted, containerized, and reverse-proxied deployments.

### 2. Multi Round-Trip Requests (MRTR) replaces open-stream elicitation

Server-initiated requests (e.g. "approve this deployment", "confirm this refund") previously depended on an open stream. MCP v2 replaces this with `input_required` results: the server returns what it needs, the client collects it, and retries the operation. No long-lived streams to balance or time out.

### 3. HTTP infrastructure understands MCP

The spec now requires `Mcp-Method` and `Mcp-Name` headers on Streamable HTTP requests. Gateways, rate limiters, and WAFs can make routing/rate-limit decisions from headers without parsing JSON bodies. It also adds `ttlMs` and `cacheScope` hints to `tools/list`/`prompts/list`/`resources/list`, with deterministically ordered tool catalogs — so clients can cache tool lists and keep caches stable across reconnects.

### 4. Tightened authorization

- Prefers pre-registered clients, then Client ID Metadata Documents (CIMD), with Dynamic Client Registration (DCR) deprecated (removal after summer 2027).
- Adopts RFC 9207 issuer identification (`authorization_response_iss_parameter_supported`) to prevent authorization-response confusion.
- Clients send the canonical server URI as the RFC 8707 `resource` in auth/token requests, so tokens are scoped to the correct audience.

### 5. Formal feature lifecycle

Features are now classified Active / Deprecated / Removed, with a minimum 12-month migration window. Roots, Sampling, Logging, DCR, and the legacy HTTP+SSE transport are deprecated but supported — giving us a clear, non-breaking migration path.

### 6. New SDKs

The TypeScript SDK was replatformed from Node.js to Web Standards (better Bun/Deno/Workers interop), split into smaller packages, and `createMcpHandler` graduated into the official SDK. The `/mcp` endpoint accepts both the new protocol and 2025 Streamable HTTP clients, so most clients reconnect without config changes.

## Why Homarr should do it

- **Simpler deployment & ops**: Our MCP server currently relies on `AsyncLocalStorage` for per-request caller context and a module-level rate-limit store. A stateless protocol removes session-related complexity and makes the endpoint behave like any other HTTP route.
- **Better scaling & reliability**: No sticky sessions means requests can hit any instance behind a load balancer / reverse proxy without session affinity — important for self-hosters running multiple replicas.
- **Caching wins**: Deterministic, cacheable `tools/list` results reduce repeated tool-catalog extraction on every connect.
- **Future-proofing**: DCR is being removed; adopting CIMD / pre-registered clients now avoids a forced migration later.
- **Ecosystem alignment**: Major clients (Claude, Cursor, VS Code Copilot, Claude Code) are moving to v2. Staying current keeps Homarr's MCP server working with the latest clients.

## Current implementation (for reference)

- `apps/nextjs/src/app/api/mcp/[transport]/route.ts` — `createMcpHandler` from `mcp-handler`, `ListToolsRequestSchema`/`CallToolRequestSchema` from `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`, plus `AsyncLocalStorage`-based caller context and a module-level auth rate-limit store.
- `apps/nextjs/src/app/api/mcp/_extract-tools.ts` — `trpc-to-mcp` tool extraction.
- `apps/nextjs/src/app/api/assistant/chat/route.ts` — the built-in Assistant consumes the same MCP tool definitions.
- `apps/nextjs/src/app/.well-known/oauth-authorization-server/route.ts` — OAuth authorization server metadata (currently advertises `registration_endpoint` for DCR).
- Docs: `apps/docs/docs/management/mcp.mdx`.

## Dependencies to bump

- `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` — currently `1.29.0` in `pnpm-workspace.yaml` catalog
- `mcp-handler` — currently `^1.1.0`
- `trpc-to-mcp` — currently `^1.3.2`

## Proposed scope

- [ ] Upgrade `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk` to the v2 (2026-07-28) release and migrate the handler to the stateless API.
- [ ] Replace/remove the `AsyncLocalStorage` caller-context pattern if the new SDK no longer needs it.
- [ ] Add `Mcp-Method` / `Mcp-Name` header support and `ttlMs`/`cacheScope` hints on `tools/list`.
- [ ] Evaluate OAuth changes: move from DCR toward CIMD / pre-registered clients; update `.well-known/oauth-authorization-server` metadata accordingly.
- [ ] Update `apps/docs/docs/management/mcp.mdx` (protocol version in curl examples, transport/auth tables, caching notes).
- [ ] Verify the built-in Assistant (`assistant/chat/route.ts`) still works with the upgraded tool extraction.

## References

- Spec: https://modelcontextprotocol.io/specification/2026-07-28
- Cloudflare announcement: https://blog.cloudflare.com/mcp-v2/
- MCP TypeScript SDK migration guide (referenced in the Cloudflare post)

title: perf: cut dashboard memory ~34% — V8 young-gen bound, server-dep unbundling, integration tree-shaking
body:
# Phase 1 + 2 — memory reduction, measured end to end

**Idle live heap −37%, peak server memory −20%, peak during multi-tab use −29%, transient
off-heap buffers −93%, browser event listeners −23%, React fibers −31%** — verified on a
restored real backup (4 boards, 51 widgets, 11 integrations) driven through a real login, not
on an empty container.

Phase 2 profiled the container at its **memory high-water mark** rather than at idle, which is
what every earlier round measured, and that changed the conclusions. It found one integration
downloading a 46 MiB JSON body per widget refresh, a 16 MiB WebAssembly heap for SSH ciphers in
an app with no SSH feature, a gRPC stack reachable only from `docker build`, and Next preloading
the module graph of all 74 routes at startup.

Every number is reproducible with `scripts/benchmarks/stress-restore.mts`, added here. Full
write-up, including a complete breakdown of one peak moment, what measured at zero, and what was
tried and rejected: [`PHASE2-FINDINGS.md`](./PHASE2-FINDINGS.md).

## Server RAM: merge-base vs this branch, end to end

This is the number that matters and the only one measured against the merge-base with everything
in place. Two runs per side, alternated, same restored backup: 4 tabs across 2 boards, 3 reloads
each, widget interaction, 2-minute idle soak. `before` = merge-base `06724cfeb`, `after` = this
branch.

**Cgroup anonymous memory** leads because it is what counts against a container limit and cannot
be reclaimed. `memory.current` is reported too but never led with: it includes page cache, which
has swung 60+ MiB between runs of a byte-identical image.

| stage | before | after | change | before spread / after spread |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **peak anon** | 376.6 MiB | **279.3 MiB** | **−26%** | [381.2, 372.0] / [253.0, 305.6] |
| boot idle | 130.5 MiB | **62.4 MiB** | **−52%** | [143.1, 117.9] / [62.1, 62.7] |
| after sign-in | 247.4 MiB | **142.9 MiB** | **−42%** | [248.7, 246.2] / [143.0, 142.9] |
| dashboard loaded | 293.4 MiB | **170.4 MiB** | **−42%** | [331.9, 254.9] / [147.8, 193.0] |
| 4 tabs, 2 boards | 366.5 MiB | **258.2 MiB** | **−30%** | [361.0, 372.0] / [253.0, 263.4] |
| after 2 min idle soak | 323.7 MiB | **200.8 MiB** | **−38%** | [313.6, 333.8] / [198.6, 203.0] |
| peak node RSS | 430.7 MiB | **336.2 MiB** | **−22%** | [434.1, 427.3] / [310.5, 361.9] |

Every stage improves and no before/after range overlaps. Unlike the earlier version of this
description, the multi-tab case improves too — that was the caveat Phase 1 had to make, and the
Umami fix removed it.

### What it costs

| metric | before | after | reliability |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| container CPU over the run | 23.5 s | **27.7 s (+18%)** | solid — [22.7, 24.3] vs [27.1, 28.3], non-overlapping |
| median board load | 540 ms | 700 ms (+30%) | **not established** — see below |
| image size | 430 MB | **417 MB** | −3% |

**+18% CPU is real** and expected: `preloadEntriesOnStart: false` moves route compilation from
boot to first use, and the Umami paging change turns one large request into several small ones.

**The +30% board load is not a reliable figure.** Individual loads were [506, 383, 1233] and
[848, 431, 574] before, against [780, 808, 515] and [621, 579, 1004] after. The ranges overlap
heavily and there is no cold-then-warm pattern — the slowest load is third in one run and first in
another. Six samples per side cannot separate a real 30% regression from this variance. If the
latency trade matters for a decision, it needs its own measurement with many more samples; the
suspicion is that it is genuine and concentrated in `preloadEntriesOnStart`.

### Which change contributed what

Measured individually, each against the build immediately before it:

| change | size | server RAM effect |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Umami: stop fetching 100k raw events per refresh** | 1 file | **−20% peak, −29% multi-tab peak, −93% transient buffers** |
| **`preloadEntriesOnStart: false`** | 1 line | **−30% anon at boot idle**, −9% after sign-in, −4% dashboard loaded, peak unchanged |
| **ssh2's 16 MiB WASM heap** (docker-modem patch) | 1 patch | **−15 to −18 MiB external**, every stage |
| **dockerode's gRPC stack** (dockerode patch) | 1 patch | −6 MiB RSS on require; **not separately visible in a full run** |
| `--max-semi-space-size=4` | 1 line | −19% idle, −21% peak (Phase 1) |
| `serverExternalPackages` (mysql2/pg + 8 more) | 1 block | −21 MiB idle, −18 MiB loaded (Phase 1) |
| V8 old-space cap | 1 line | 0 — a drift ceiling, not a reduction |
| cache-invalidation layer + `next-cache-handler` | ~30 files | **0 — deleted** |

The gRPC row is honest about its limits: it removes 112 files and 6 MiB from an isolated
`require`, but the end-to-end A/B cannot separate it from the other changes, so treat it as bundle
hygiene with a plausible small win rather than a measured one.

## How it was measured

`scripts/benchmarks/stress-restore.mts` boots a fresh container, restores a supplied
backup **through the onboarding restore UI** (including typing "I understand"), signs in,
opens boards across several tabs, clicks into widgets, reloads, then soaks idle —
sampling cgroup memory, CPU, browser heap, DOM nodes and listeners at each stage.

Each run proves it is actually behind a login rather than reading a public page: it
asserts a cookie-less request to the private board is **denied**, requires the Auth.js
session cookie after sign-in, and reports whether it modified the restored data at all
(currently `none`).

Measurement bugs found and fixed along the way, all of which had produced wrong numbers:

- `memory.current` counts reclaimable page cache and swung **192–261 MiB for the same
  image**. Comparisons use anonymous memory, stable to ±2 MiB.
- Playwright clicks fired **before hydration** were silent no-ops that looked like
  auth failures.
- A context-menu gate using `click({ button: "right" })` emitted no `contextmenu`
  event, so it failed *shipped code* identically — it wrongly condemned one optimisation
  before being fixed and re-validated against the un-optimised build.

The backup is passed by path via `STRESS_BACKUP_ZIP` and never enters the repo — it
carries real integration secrets. `.gitignore` also refuses `homarr-backup*.zip` and
loose `*.sqlite`.

## Dashboard rendering: a systemic Mantine cost, found in five places

Full write-up: [`docs/perf/CLIENT-PERFORMANCE.md`](./docs/perf/CLIENT-PERFORMANCE.md).

**Mantine overlay components mount their full machinery regardless of `disabled`.** A `Tooltip`,
`HoverCard` or `Popover` that can never open still creates a `Popover`, a `PopoverTarget` and a
`PopoverDropdown`. `disabled` suppresses *display*, not *cost* — so avoiding it means deciding before
rendering, not passing a prop.

That single fact accounts for five separate findings, three of them measured:

| widget | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **mediaReleases** | 340 components / 8,387 fibers | **170 / 8,057** (−50% components) |
| **calendar** | 171 components / 1,195 fibers | **75 / 907** (−56% components, −24% fibers) |
| **beszelSystemTable** | 36 components / 1,286 fibers | **18 / 1,230** (−50% components) |
| downloads, mediaRequests, app | unchanged | unchanged — their overlays are functional |

- **calendar** mounted a `HoverCard` per day cell. A month grid is ~42 cells and `disabled` is
  `isEditMode || eventsForDate.length === 0`, so most days — and in edit mode *every* day — mounted
  three components for a card that can never open. 126 of its 171 components, in a widget with only
  251 DOM nodes.
- **OverflowBadge** (shared UI in `packages/ui`) mounted a `Popover` and `Popover.Dropdown` even when
  nothing overflowed, which is the common case. Used by media-releases, releases, the docker table and
  the widget inputs, so it repeated per row wherever a list renders it. This is where the entire
  media-releases win came from.
- **beszel disk-usage** mounted a `HoverCard` per table row for systems reporting no filesystems —
  it already fell back to a plain bar inside its own target, so the overlay existed to render nothing.

### Two remount bugs

A component declared inside a render body is a **new type every render**, so React unmounts and
remounts its subtree instead of updating it.

- `beszelSystemTable` declared `PercentCell` inline and used it for three columns, while the widget
  re-renders ~1×/second from its live subscription — three cell subtrees per system rebuilt every
  second. Hoisted and memoised.
- A drag handle was passed to a child as `handle={Handle}` while its parent re-renders every frame of
  a drag, so the handle was rebuilt continuously mid-drag. Stabilised with `useMemo`.

### The audit that found them

`scripts/benchmarks/audit-widget-render.mjs` scans every widget and ranks findings by whether they sit
inside a `.map()`, since those multiply by row count. All 54 findings were triaged:

| count | pattern | outcome |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 12 | overlay-per-row | **5 fixed**; the other 7 are functional tooltips with real labels — nothing is disabled to skip, and swapping them for native `title` would change UX, not just cost |
| 11 | index-key | **all safe.** Either static text splits (`description.split("\n")`) or stateless read-only rows from user-configured JSONPath data with no stable id, where an index key is correct and avoids remounts |
| 2 | nested-component | **both fixed** |
| 29 | inline-style-per-row | **left alone.** A fresh object per row only defeats memoisation if the child is memoised, and these are not. 29 edits without a measurement is churn |

### Off-screen rendering

`mediaReleases` rendered **80 cards into a 539 px tile whose content is 7,206 px** — 7 visible, 73
off-screen, each still fetching and decoding a poster and a full-tile backdrop. Decoded bitmaps are
far larger in memory than their files, which is what made this expensive.

Fixed with `content-visibility: auto` + `contain-intrinsic-size`, plus `loading="lazy"`. Three repeats
per side:

| metric | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| image requests | 135, 135, 135 | **55, 55, 56** (−59%) |
| image bytes | 12.27 MiB | **8.41 MiB** (−31%) |
| layout objects | 8346, 7815, 7815 | **5117, 4696, 4636** (−41%) |

Extracted to `offscreenRowStyle()` and applied to the other data-driven lists (rssFeed, notifications,
calendar events, media-requests). Applied to 5 of 26 `ScrollArea` widgets deliberately:
`content-visibility` costs containment work and can be wrong on self-measuring content like charts.

### Two metrics that cannot be used, and one claim withdrawn

**Chrome's board-level `JSEventListeners` is unusable here.** Across six runs of identical code it read
7905, 8000, 8166, 8179, 10360 and 17114. Its `Nodes` counter has the same problem — 23,072 on one run
against ~8,850 on the others — because it counts detached nodes awaiting collection, while
"elements under body" stayed at 6,691–6,726 throughout. Only per-widget component and fiber counts are
stable enough to compare, so those are what is reported above.

**The media-releases tooltip fix measured zero**, and is reported as such. Every release on the test
board has a description and the option is on, so all 80 tooltips are legitimately enabled and none are
skipped. The mechanism is correct; this board is not the case it helps. The −50% for that widget came
entirely from OverflowBadge.

### Idle churn is legitimate, and an earlier claim here was wrong

This description previously said ~80% of idle React commits entered at Next's `HeadManagerContext` and
that the App Router re-rendered once a second. **Both were false.** A 3-item board commits **0.0**
times per minute against 76.0 for the 28-item board — if the router re-rendered on a timer, every board
would churn. The original attribution was a tooling artefact: `fiber.actualDuration` is only populated
by a React *profiling* build, so on production every fiber fails the "did it re-render" test and the
tables come back empty, which reads as "nothing" rather than "this build cannot tell you".

Attributed properly, three Beszel widgets are 82% of idle churn — but the real rate is **1.22 commits
per second** for the whole board at **13.3 DOM mutations per commit**. That is three live-monitoring
widgets refreshing about once a second, which is what they are for. A coalescing fix measured *exactly
zero* (55 commits both sides) and was reverted.

## What Next.js itself costs

Stated plainly because the framework was assumed to be the problem. Next's loaded source is **flat at
3.47 MiB** and does not grow at all between boot and a fully loaded multi-tab session, while the
application's own chunks grow four-fold:

| stage | total | next/dist | vendored | Homarr's chunks |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| boot idle | 10.56 MiB | 1.75 (359f) | 1.58 (25f) | 3.73 (28f) |
| multi-tab | 22.89 MiB | **1.80 (364f)** | **1.67 (32f)** | **15.44 (241f)** |

So the ~41 MiB of retained bundle source is overwhelmingly **this application's** code. The one
Next-side change that mattered was configuration, not code.

## Status, and one item that is not verified

`c526dd2b7` applies the same `content-visibility` treatment to `mediaRequests-requestList` (the only
other widget that genuinely overdraws: 1,512 px of cards in a 405 px tile, 60 images). It is
typechecked but **not measured** — it is the single performance claim on this branch that was not
A/B'd before commit. [`docs/perf/NEXT-STEPS.md`](./docs/perf/NEXT-STEPS.md) has the exact command to
verify it and says to revert it if image requests do not fall.

That handoff also records the one lever with real headroom left — the tRPC router's eager integration
imports, a **16.10 MiB subtree of 460 files** reached by every API route, which pays twice because
both the retained source and the compiler-zone memory scale with how much JavaScript the server
compiles.

## Profiling build

```bash
pnpm docker:profiling
```

`docker build . -t homarr:performance` alone produces a **non-profiling** image. Four
things had to line up, each failing silently: `reactProductionProfiling` is webpack-only;
Turbopack needs `next build --profile`; turbo strips env vars not declared in the task's
`env`; and Next applies the React swap through a webpack alias Turbopack never sees, so
the Dockerfile now performs that swap on the vendored entry, guarded to fail loudly.

## The bug that was most of the peak

`arrayBuffers` went **0.3 → 94.3 → 2.0 MiB** across a session — entirely transient, which is
exactly why memory appeared to oscillate between ~835 MB and ~400 MB and never settle. Soak
growth was **−102 MiB/hour**, so there was no leak.

Tracking large allocations by stack found **48.3 MiB at one site, including a single 46.3 MiB
allocation**, inside undici's `fullyReadBody` — the machinery behind `Response.json()`, which
holds the socket chunk list *and* the joined copy at the same instant, so a body of size N
costs about 2N. Capturing the bytes identified it immediately:

```
46.3 MiB assembled from 3,946 socket chunks
{"data":[{"id":"1251f6db…","websiteId":"f133f10c…","sessionId":"9e02d227…","createdAt":"2026-08-09T…
```

Umami. Two call sites requested `pageSize: "100000"` — up to 100,000 raw event records — and
`getMultiEventTimeSeriesAsync` ran them for **every tracked event name concurrently** via
`Promise.all`. `getEventNamesAsync` was downloading every raw event of the last 30 days *to
collect a handful of distinct name strings*.

| call site | before | after |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `getEventNamesAsync` | list 100k raw events, collect distinct names | aggregated `/metrics?type=event`, one row per name |
| `getWebsiteEventTimeSeriesAsync` | one page of up to 100k records | pages of 5,000, folded into buckets and released |
| `getMultiEventTimeSeriesAsync` | `Promise.all` over all event names | sequential |

Instances returning aggregated `{x,y}` buckets still answer in one request; an instance that
accepts `pageSize` but ignores `page` is detected and stopped rather than double-counted; and
hitting the page ceiling logs a warning instead of silently undercounting. Covered by 6 new
tests — there were none for this integration before.

#### Measured result

Alternated runs, 2 before and 2 after, same harness and workload. Per-run spread is shown
because it is what decides whether a difference means anything.

| metric | before | after | change | before / after spread |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| **peak container** | 498.9 MiB | **398.5 MiB** | **−20%** | [461.6, 536.3] / [387.0, 410.0] |
| **peak node RSS** | 452.4 MiB | **353.3 MiB** | **−22%** | [432.7, 472.2] / [355.6, 350.9] |
| **peak during 4 tabs** | 498.5 MiB | **356.3 MiB** | **−29%** | [460.8, 536.3] / [341.8, 370.8] |
| **peak arrayBuffers** | 95.8 MiB | **6.6 MiB** | **−93%** | [95.7, 95.8] / [6.4, 6.7] |
| largest single allocation | 46.4 MiB | **2.4 MiB** | −95% | identical in both runs |
| median board load | 526 ms | 523 ms | no change | overlapping |
| CPU over the run | 19.5 s | 20.4 s | +4% | the extra round trips |

Every peak metric separates cleanly — the two sides' ranges do not overlap. Two rows
deliberately do **not** support a claim: post-soak steady state (324.2 → 322.5 MiB) is
inconclusive, and boot idle is noise — its spread is ±20 MiB on *identical* code, and Umami's
code is not even loaded at boot.

Widget readiness is identical before and after (28/28 on the board carrying the three Umami
widgets), so nothing broke. The "after" container log does contain one line the "before" runs
could not produce:

```
warn: Event time series hit the page ceiling, counts are a lower bound
      eventName="Add app" maxRecords="100000"
```

That site really does have >100,000 events for one event name. **The old code had the same
100k ceiling** — that is what the 46.3 MiB body was — but it truncated silently and reported
the undercount as fact. The ceiling is unchanged; it is now visible. That event name is also
the worst case for round trips (20 sequential requests) and it still did not move board load
latency.

## A full breakdown of one peak moment

Everything below is one instant: the high-water mark of a real session — backup restored,
signed in, four tabs across two boards, widgets polling. **Node RSS 357.8 MiB.**

Peak is `nav-01`, not the multi-tab stage. A GC lands during multi-tab and pulls RSS *down*,
so "most tabs open" is not "most memory". Measuring the wrong stage understates peak by 37 MiB.

### First: why a heap snapshot cannot answer this

V8 runs a full GC before serialising a snapshot, so a snapshot reports **survivors only**. The
94 MiB of ArrayBuffers that used to drive this container past 500 MB never appeared in one.
Three instruments were needed, and each is blind to what the others see:

| instrument | sees | blind to |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `HeapProfiler.startSampling` (in-process `inspector.Session`) | every V8-heap allocation, survivor or garbage, with a stack | anything outside the V8 heap — including all `Buffer` backing stores |
| wrapped `Buffer.alloc`/`concat` | external buffer allocations, with a stack and content preview | V8-heap objects |
| `/proc/<pid>/smaps`, captured every stage | JS heap vs JIT vs native vs file-backed pages | anything below page granularity |

The Umami bug was invisible to the first and obvious to the second.

### View A — the operating system's view

From `/proc/<pid>/smaps`. This sums to RSS exactly. Anonymous mappings are classified by
signature: V8 allocates its heap in 256 KiB pages (`kRegularPageSize`) and nothing else in the
process allocates at that granularity in bulk; pthread reserves ~8 MiB per thread stack and
touches almost none of it.

| mapping bucket | MiB | share | what it is |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| V8 heap pages (256 KiB each) | 153.1 | 43% | the JS heap proper |
| other anonymous | 118.8 | 34% | V8's large-object space + external buffers + real malloc |
| **node binary text** | **65.7** | **19%** | the Node runtime's own code — file-backed, shared between processes, and **not counted in cgroup `anon`** |
| JIT code (anonymous executable) | 10.1 | 3% | machine code V8 compiled; 1.9 MiB at boot |
| shared libraries | 2.8 | 1% | |
| native addons | 2.0 | 1% | better_sqlite3 + bcrypt |
| malloc brk heap | 1.5 | — | |
| thread stacks | 0.4 | — | 48 MiB *reserved*, essentially untouched |
| **total** | **354.5** | | matches RSS |

That 65.7 MiB is the single most misread number in this whole exercise. It is why RSS reads
139 MiB at boot while cgroup `anon` reads 89 MiB, and it is not a cost this application can
influence — it is the Node binary, shared and reclaimable.

V8 additionally **reserves 16.8 GiB of address space**. That is not memory.

### View B — V8's own accounting

| component | MiB | notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `heapUsed` — live JS objects | 175.7 | broken down below |
| ├ old_space | 123.4 | long-lived objects |
| ├ large_object_space | 34.5 | objects over the page threshold — mostly bundled source strings |
| ├ code_space | 9.0 | compiled code metadata |
| ├ trusted_space | 8.5 | |
| └ new_space | 0.1 | of 8.0 MiB committed — young-generation churn is *not* the problem |
| `heapTotal − heapUsed` | 12.3 | committed to the heap but currently free |
| `external` | 24.6 | Buffers and ArrayBuffers off-heap |
| everything else | 145.2 | node binary + JIT + native malloc + libs + stacks |

Cross-checked rather than assumed: `heapTotal 188.0 − the 256 KiB pages 153.1 = 34.9 MiB`,
matching `large_object_space` at 34.5. So the handful of very large anonymous mappings
(31.6, 20.7, 8.4 MiB) are V8's large-object space — **not** the runaway native allocator their
shape first suggested.

### View C — what those 175.7 MiB of live objects actually are

From a post-GC snapshot taken at peak with all tabs still open (1.43 M nodes):

| bucket | MiB | why it exists |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **strings** | **51.1** | **~41 MiB is bundled JavaScript source**, retained because V8 keeps a script's source alive while any function in it may still be lazily compiled |
| ArrayBuffer backing stores | 17.8 | socket and HTTP buffers |
| object property arrays | 10.6 | app state |
| object element arrays | 6.1 | |
| shapes / maps / descriptors | 6.6 | V8 bookkeeping for object shapes |
| closures | 5.7 | |
| plain objects | 4.9 | |
| concatenated strings | 3.3 | |
| contexts | 2.7 | closure scopes |
| compiled-code metadata | ~12 | bytecode, feedback vectors, scope info |

### The single most important structural fact

**The retained heap at peak is the same as at rest.** A post-GC snapshot at peak is 160.7 MiB
of shallow size; after a 60-second idle soak it is 157.7 MiB. Strings 51.1 vs 50.1 MiB.
Nothing accumulates — soak growth is **−102 MiB/hour**.

So the peak is not retention. It is transient churn plus pages V8 and malloc have not returned
to the OS. That is precisely why memory appears to "oscillate between 835 MB and 400 MB" and
never settles at the high mark, and it means **no cache-tuning or `gcTime` change can help** —
which is exactly what every such attempt measured at zero.

And after the Umami fix the churn is small: total V8-heap allocation across an entire run is
**125 MiB**, 40% of it Node's own module loader reading source files, and the whole four-tab
burst allocates **3.3 MiB**.

### An observer effect, recorded because it produced a fake finding

The first peak snapshot was taken over CDP, which delivers it as JS string chunks. For a
~135 MB snapshot that added **~134 MiB of ArrayBuffers to the process being measured**, and the
next stage read 693.7 MiB — a number that looks exactly like an application problem. The
`native malloc / buffers` row jumping to 374.6 MiB at `05-after-stress` in the per-stage table
is the same artefact. `v8.writeHeapSnapshot` streams from C++ instead, and the probe now
reports its own `observerCostMiB` so the cost of looking is never assumed to be zero.

## What was chopped, and what was measured and left alone

Every row is measured. The rejected ones are listed with their price and the reason, because
"we tried it and it costs more than it saves" is a result.

### Shipped

| chop | measured effect | how |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Umami: 100k raw events per widget refresh** | **−20% peak, −29% multi-tab peak, −93% transient buffers**, largest allocation 46.4 → 2.4 MiB | aggregated `/metrics` endpoint, 5,000-record paging, sequential fan-out |
| **Next preloading all 74 route graphs at boot** | **−37% live heap at idle** (70.7 → 44.8 MiB), −13.4 MiB source, **310 fewer files even at full load** | `experimental.preloadEntriesOnStart: false` |
| **ssh2's 16 MiB ChaCha20-Poly1305 WASM heap** | **−15 to −18 MiB external**, every stage, four runs, non-overlapping | pnpm patch: `docker-modem` requires `./ssh` inside the `protocol === 'ssh'` branch that already guarded its only use |
| **dockerode's gRPC stack (112 files)** | requiring dockerode: 26.6 → **20.6 MiB RSS**, grpc 63 → 0 files, protobufjs 49 → 0 | pnpm patch: `./session` required inside `buildImage`, its only call site |
| cache-invalidation layer + `next-cache-handler` | 0 — nothing imported it | deleted, 883 lines / 18 files |

### Measured, understood, and deliberately not shipped

| candidate | prize | why not |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **ASCII-escape server bundles** | **9.45 MiB** | One character above U+00FF forces V8 to store a whole source string at 2 bytes/char. Proven directly: `✅` twice in a 538 KB chunk costs +527 KiB. Recovering it means rewriting minified **vendor** output at build time inside the production image. That deserves its own PR and its own safety argument. |
| **Lazy-load mysql2 and pg** (both load on every SQLite install) | **21.4 MiB** | Three attempts, each caught only by booting the real image. `createRequire(import.meta.url)` is `undefined` in the CommonJS `migrate.cjs` bundle and broke startup for *every* dialect. A dynamic require resolves to a `.cjs` build Next never traces. Leaving drizzle's dialect static defeats it, because `drizzle-orm/mysql2` imports `mysql2` itself. The remaining routes either load a **second copy of drizzle's core** beside the ESM one, or hardcode drizzle's internal file layout so an upgrade breaks startup for MySQL and Postgres. Structural blocker: `createDb` must stay synchronous because `packages/db/index.ts` does `export const db = createDb(schema)` at module scope and `migrate.cjs` is CommonJS. |
| Redis 6 → 2 client consolidation | 0.1 MiB | inside noise; reverted. The `pubSub:last:*` TTL was kept as a genuine unbounded-growth fix. |
| V8 old-space cap | 0 | removing it entirely matched the capped build at every stage. Kept as one line because it bounds the #5301 drift case. |
| `--max-semi-space-size=2` (vs the shipped 4) | 0 | no improvement. |
| base64 images in cache / TanStack Query / Redis | 0.01 MiB | the theory that started this: **2 data-URLs**, Redis totals 2.17 MB, `image-proxy` stores URL + headers and never image bytes. |

### `--jitless`: the most tempting result in the whole exercise, and it is not real

V8's `--jitless` removes the optimising compiler and all generated machine code. It applies
cleanly through `NODE_OPTIONS` and the effect on code memory is unambiguous — **code space
11.6 → 0.0 MiB**. The stress numbers looked spectacular: peak node RSS −24%, peak container
−36%, CPU −14%, median board load **30% faster**.

Three of those are impossible. `--jitless` was applied to the **server**, so it cannot make the
*browser* lighter, and removing an optimising compiler does not make code run faster. The client
metrics explain it:

| | normal | jitless |
| --- | --- | --- |
| DOM nodes | 8,256 / 8,280 | **5,442 / 5,442** |
| JS event listeners | 7,781 / 7,784 | **1,570 / 1,570** |
| browser JS heap | 50.0 / 49.5 MiB | 28.1 / 28.2 MiB |
| widget controls available | 244 | 216 |

Boards still reported 28/28 widgets ready, so the coarse check passed — but the page carries
**80% fewer event listeners**. A large part of the UI never mounted. The apparent memory win is
an app that did less work, and the CPU and latency "improvements" are the same thing.

**Rejected.** Recorded because the tell generalises: when a server-side change moves a
client-side metric, the workload changed, and the comparison is void.

### jemalloc: tested, and musl turns out to be the frugal one

The largest attributed-but-unfixed item is ~38 MiB of V8 parser/compiler zone memory that is freed
back to malloc and never returned to the kernel by musl. An allocator that decays unused spans back
to the OS looked like the obvious answer.

Tested on the **byte-identical image**, with jemalloc activated only by `HOMARR_MALLOC=jemalloc`
via `LD_PRELOAD`, so both sides differed by one environment variable and nothing else — no
build-to-build variance. The "Using jemalloc" log line was asserted present, so this is not
inferred from the variable being set.

| stage | musl | jemalloc |
| --- | --- | --- |
| boot idle | 62.4 MiB | **80.3 MiB (+29%)** |
| after sign-in | 144.9 MiB | **170.6 MiB (+18%)** |
| dashboard loaded | 214.8 MiB | 184.4 MiB (−14%) |
| 4 tabs | 259.9 MiB | **319.6 MiB (+23%)** |
| after soak | 215.5 MiB | **279.6 MiB (+30%)** |
| **CPU** | 28.0 s | **24.5 s (−13%)** |

Every row non-overlapping. **The hypothesis was backwards**: jemalloc does not release freed spans
sooner, it deliberately retains more of them (thread-local caches plus time-based dirty-page decay)
and spends that memory on speed. Reverted. This closes off "swap the allocator" as a RAM direction —
musl is already the frugal choice. If CPU ever becomes the binding constraint, it is a measured 13%
for two lines.

### Not reachable through `NODE_OPTIONS`

`--optimize-for-size`, `--no-opt` and `--lite-mode` are all rejected by Node with
"not allowed in NODE_OPTIONS", so they cannot be offered as a runtime knob without changing how
the server is invoked. Only `--jitless` and `--max-semi-space-size` are usable.

### What remains, in order of size

1. **~41 MiB of retained bundle source** (28% of the live heap). Still the largest single item.
   `preloadEntriesOnStart` took 6.3 MiB off it permanently; the rest needs the tRPC router to
   stop referencing every integration eagerly — a 16 MiB subtree reached by every API route.
2. **~59 MiB of native malloc at peak**, the least understood remaining bucket. Not V8's
   large-object space (that was checked and ruled out).
3. **The client, not the server.** A real multi-tab session reaches a 650 MB browser heap with
   71,596 live fibers. The idle-churn part of that is now attributed and fixed (Beszel, above);
   what remains is the render cost of the board itself under interaction, which is larger than
   everything on the server side.

## Corrections to numbers this PR previously reported

Measurement bugs of my own, listed because each one had produced a figure in an earlier version
of this description.

**"7.86 MiB of literal duplicate chunk sources" was wrong.** It came from grouping heap-snapshot
strings by content, but V8 **truncates string contents to ~1 KiB when serialising a snapshot**,
so the comparison only ever saw each string's first kilobyte and reported near-identical chunks
as identical. Hashing the real files found **zero byte-identical duplicates among all 3,055
server JS files (77.6 MiB)**.

The real doubling has a different cause. A V8 string is either 1 byte per character or 2, and
**one character above U+00FF forces the entire source string to two bytes**. 80 of 1,105 loaded
files (9.45 MiB) contain one, costing 18.91 MiB of heap. Proven directly rather than inferred, by
reading one chunk as shipped and again with its non-Latin-1 characters replaced by `?` — identical
length, so the only variable is character width:

```
_049nb9n._.js   538,519 chars, 2 of them non-Latin-1
  as shipped    : 2.00 bytes/char  (1053 KiB per copy)
  ascii variant : 1.00 bytes/char  ( 526 KiB per copy)
```

Two characters — `process.versions.icu?"✅":"Y "` — cost 527 KiB. The rest are zod's `✖`, a `💩`
UTF-8 self-test, and Next's `○ ⨯ ⚠` log symbols. Predicted total 31.16 MiB against 32.43 MiB
measured, within 4%.

**The require-cost sweep was measured without forcing a GC**, so its figures included V8 growing
its heap opportunistically rather than each module's real cost. Re-measured with `global.gc()`
before every reading: the unused database drivers cost **21.4 MiB**, not the ~30 MiB the naive sum
implied, and `drizzle-orm`'s headline 124.3 MiB was almost entirely the artefact. The ssh2
conclusion is unaffected — it was confirmed independently by the before/after external-memory drop.

**"+24.1 MiB for dockerode's gRPC stack" was a bare-process figure.** In context it is 6.0 MiB;
most of the cost overlaps with what dockerode loads anyway. The patch comment records the
in-context number.

**Route preloading was previously written off as "framework behaviour, not something this codebase
sets."** That was wrong — `experimental.preloadEntriesOnStart` exists for exactly this, and turning
it off is the largest idle-memory win in this PR.

## What is left, and an honest correction about it

Earlier versions of this description named a **16.10 MiB subtree of 460 files reached by every API
route** as the one remaining server-side lever, blaming the tRPC router for importing every integration
eagerly. **Both halves were wrong**, and finding that out is part of the result.

**The integration creator was already fully lazy.** Every kind in
`packages/integrations/src/base/creator.ts` is `() => import(...)` — no integration class loads until
one is constructed. The earlier barrel diet had already done this; the claim was never checked against
the code.

**The subtree was an artefact of route preloading**, measured before `preloadEntriesOnStart: false`
shipped, when Next loaded all 74 routes' graphs at startup. That fix removed it. Re-measured on the
current build, boot is **706 files / 10.56 MiB**:

| owner | size | files | reducible? |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `.next/server/chunks` (app code) | 3.73 MiB | 28 | already lean at 28 chunks |
| better-sqlite3 | 2.16 MiB | 14 | no — 2.1 MiB is the native binary, and it is the default driver |
| next/dist + compiled | 3.33 MiB | 384 | no — framework, flat regardless of load |
| **mysql2 + pg** | **0.52 MiB** | 90 | in principle yes; structurally blocked, see above |

**So there is no single large server lever left.** What remains is diffuse: a full multi-tab session
loads **15.44 MiB of the app's own chunks across 241 files**, and both the ~41 MiB of retained source
and the ~38 MiB of compiler zones scale with exactly that. Reducing it means shipping less application
JavaScript per route — a broad refactor with no single target, not a subtree waiting to be cut.

Avenues that are closed, each with numbers in [`REJECTED.md`](./docs/perf/REJECTED.md): every V8 flag
(`--jitless` fakes a win by under-rendering, `--max-opt` is null because Maglev's zones match
Turbofan's, three more are rejected by Node outright), the allocator (jemalloc costs 18–30% *more*
resident memory), zlib orphans (do not occur here), native contexts (0.25 MiB each), sharp (never
loads), and base64 caching (0.01 MiB).

## What was removed for measuring zero

- **`packages/next-cache-handler`** — orphaned; nothing imported it.
- **`cache-tags` / `cache-invalidation` and 66 `revalidateTag` call sites** — no
  `"use cache"`, `cacheTag` or `unstable_cache` exists in app source, so these fired on
  tags nothing registers. Removing them also removed the `SELECT`s that existed only to
  feed them, returning six routers to the merge-base exactly.
- **Redis 6 → 2 client consolidation** — 139.3 vs 139.2 MiB idle. Reverted; the
  `pubSub:last:*` TTL is kept as a genuine unbounded-growth fix.
- **The V8 heap cap is a ceiling, not a reduction** — removing it entirely matched the
  capped build at every stage. Kept as one line because it bounds the #5301 drift case.

That trimming removed **883 lines and 18 files** and cost nothing on re-measurement.

## Also in here

- SVG upload sanitisation hardened: jsdom → linkedom + DOMPurify, content-based
  detection so a mislabelled upload cannot bypass it, 13-vector XSS corpus.
- Dead code: 4 unused `/api/about` routes; runtime glob over every `package.json`
  replaced with build-time static JSON.
- Widget definitions and integration clients load lazily instead of via eager barrels.
- Memory attribution tooling: `attribute-memory.mts` (cgroup → mappings → V8 spaces →
  loaded code), `memory-probe.cjs` (injectable preload; buffer- and fetch-tracking),
  `analyze-probe-stages.mjs`, `analyze-heap-dominators.mjs` (real retained sizes via a
  dominator tree), `compare-stress-runs.mjs`.

## Test plan

- [x] `pnpm test` — 1800/1801 passing; the one failure is a pre-existing Testcontainers
      flake (pi-hole / home-assistant `ECONNREFUSED` under parallel load) that passes
      11/11 when those two specs are run in isolation
- [x] 6 new tests for the Umami integration, which previously had none
- [x] Full E2E suite (8/8) against the built image with `preloadEntriesOnStart: false`
- [x] All three database dialects boot on the built image — SQLite, MySQL and Postgres each
      against a real server, on distinct ephemeral ports (a fixed port silently passed by
      hitting a leftover container the first time)
- [x] Both dependency patches verified in the image, not just in the patch file: ssh2 files
      21 → 0 and grpc 63 → 0 after `require("dockerode")`
- [x] `pnpm typecheck` — clean across 37 packages
- [x] `pnpm lint` — no new errors
- [x] **CI green end to end, including Container and E2E**
- [x] Context-menu behaviour gated by `verify-context-menu.mts` (opens on right-click,
      shows actions, closes, re-targets, touch long-press), validated by passing against
      unmodified code first
- [x] Before/after measured with one instrument, alternated, 2 runs per side

title: bug: RSS widget poster images don't load for reddit feeds
body:
### Describe the bug

I added the reddit feed (https://www.reddit.com/r/selfhosted/.rss) to the RSS widget with "Show poster image" on, and the thumbnails never render. The poster boxes show up with the alt text but the image stays empty, and the requests fail with a 403 from reddit's CDN.   
   
I found the cause in `packages/request-handler/src/rss-feeds.ts`. The parser only checks enclosure and `media:content` for images, but reddit feed uses `media:thumbnail`. Because of that it always ends up in the regex fallback in `getImageFromStringAsFallback`, which matches up to the file extension and drops the query string. That's a problem because reddit puts the s= signature in the query string and their CDN rejects the request without it, hence the 403. 
     
The extracted enclosure comes out as `https://preview.redd.it/iggp10gibfhh1.jpeg`, but the URL in the feed is `https://preview.redd.it/iggp10gibfhh1.jpeg?width=640&crop=smart&auto=webp&s=0ea9429fb5bf159b2368f906c7b7edb3246140e3`. I tested both with curl and the truncated URL returns 403 while the full one returns 200.

### Steps to reproduce

1. Add an RSS widget with https://www.reddit.com/r/selfhosted/.rss
2. Enable "Show poster image"
3. Wait for it to fetch. The poster boxes render with alt text but no image ever loads

### Impact

Not a blocker, the rest of the widget works fine, but the poster option is useless for reddit feeds. Any feed that uses `media:thumbnail` instead of enclosure or `media:content` should be affected the same way.

### Additional information

I added `media:thumbnail` to the `mediaProperties` array locally and it extracts the full signed URL, so images load. Happy to open a PR with that fix if it makes sense.

### Version

1.73.0

### Installation method

Docker Compose

### Browser

Firefox

title: feat: add UGREEN NAS (UGOS) integration
body:
## Add UGREEN NAS (UGOS) integration

Adds a new integration for UGREEN NAS devices running UGOS, following the pattern of the existing Synology, TrueNAS and Unraid integrations. Implements `ISystemHealthMonitoringIntegration`, so it plugs into the existing Health Monitoring, System Resources and System Disks widgets without any widget-side changes.

### What's included

- CPU utilization/temperature, memory usage, uptime, and system version
- Storage volume usage (used/available/percentage) per UGOS volume
- Disk SMART status and temperature, matched to volumes where the underlying pool is a single disk (see note below)

### Authentication

UGOS does not publish an official public API. This integration talks to the same internal endpoints used by the UGOS web interface (reverse-engineered from network traffic, cross-checked against the public ugos-cli and Home Assistant UGREEN NAS integration projects):

1. `POST /ugreen/v1/verify/check` with `{ username }` returns the NAS's RSA public key in the `x-rsa-token` response header (base64-encoded). Note: despite being labeled `-----BEGIN RSA PUBLIC KEY-----` (PKCS#1), the underlying ASN.1 content is actually SPKI/X.509 - this is re-wrapped with the correct generic PEM header before use.
2. The password is encrypted with that key (RSA, PKCS1v1.5 padding) using Node's built-in node:crypto, no external dependency needed.
3. `POST /ugreen/v1/verify/login` with the encrypted password returns a session token, used as a `?token=` query parameter on subsequent requests.

### Known limitations

- Multi-disk volumes report no SMART status/temperature. A UGOS volume can span multiple physical disks (e.g. a JBOD pool). Since there's no single meaningful temperature/status for such a volume, Homarr correctly displays "N/A", matching the behavior of TrueNAS/Unraid for multi-disk ZFS pools/arrays. Only volumes backed by a single physical disk get real SMART data.
- External USB disks have no SMART data available. The disk-listing endpoint (`/ugreen/v2/storage/disk/list`) only returns internal SATA/NVMe disks; external USB disks aren't included, so their volumes never get temperature/status even when the pool is single-disk.
- The `visibleStorageVolumes` widget option is Synology-only in the current codebase (`shouldHide` logic in system-disks/health-monitoring widget definitions), so it's not available for UGOS. This is a pre-existing limitation of the widget options, not something introduced by this PR - happy to extend it in a follow-up if maintainers want.
- Tested against a single device (UGREEN DXP2800, UGOS 1.17.0.0095). Endpoint behavior on other models/firmware versions is unverified.

### Icon

`iconUrl` points to `dashboard-icons/svg/ugreen.svg`, which already exists in the `homarr-labs/dashboard-icons` repository (added August 2025) - no follow-up PR needed there.

### Testing

- `pnpm build` and `pnpm format:fix` pass (run from Git Bash on Windows - invoking the Next.js build script via `turbo build` directly on Windows failed for unrelated reasons, a pre-existing shell-compatibility issue with the `HOMARR_VERSION=... pnpm with-env next build` script, not something introduced by this PR)
- `pnpm typecheck` passes across definitions, integrations, api, widgets
- Manually tested end-to-end against a physical DXP2800: login, all four data endpoints, System Resources/System Disks/Health Monitoring widgets all render correctly with live data
- Offline/unreachable smoke test: pointed the integration at an unreachable IP, saved. Connection test fails cleanly after a 10s timeout with a handled `TestConnectionError`, no crash, no hang, no unhandled exception in the server log

### Documentation

Docs were added directly in this repository under `apps/docs/docs/integrations/ugos`, mirroring the existing pattern for Synology/Unraid/TrueNAS (which also live there rather than in a separate repo). The PR template links to a separate `homarr-labs/documentation` repository for docs contributions - that appears to be outdated for integration docs specifically, since all existing integration docs I found live in this monorepo. Happy to move this if I'm missing something.

### Checklist

- [x] Integration registered in definitions, integrations, api, widgets
- [x] Documentation page added (apps/docs/docs/integrations/ugos)
- [x] Icon already available in dashboard-icons (`ugreen.svg`)
- [x] Manually tested online and offline/unreachable scenarios against a real device
- [ ] Maintainer review of the RSA auth approach and undocumented-API disclosure above

body:
## Summary

Add optional SABnzbd archived-history support to Homarr's existing Downloads widget using the widget options architecture.

This change is implemented entirely in Homarr. It does not modify SABnzbd, its queue, Archive behavior, or API.

## User-facing behavior

- Adds **Include archived SABnzbd history** to the Downloads widget when SABnzbd is selected
- Adds an **Archived history window** as a numeric widget option
- Uses positive whole-day values with 1-day increments
- Defaults the history window to **7 days**
- Archived history is **disabled by default**
- The history-window option appears only when archived history is enabled
- Existing **Limit items per integration** still controls how many rows are displayed
- Uses Homarr's existing widget option and translation systems

## Implementation

- Threads the widget options through the existing Downloads request path
- Fetches SABnzbd archived history using `archive`, `start`, and `limit`
- Uses bounded pagination with 100-item pages and a hard 100-page safety cap
- Stops on partial pages or once a full page is entirely older than the selected window
- Merges normal and archived history
- Filters to the selected date window
- Sorts newest-first
- Deduplicates by `nzo_id`

No integration-options persistence layer, database schema changes, migrations, onboarding changes, or integration management-form changes are added.

## Validation

The earlier widget-options candidate passed its focused archived-history tests, affected-workspace typechecks, lint, production Docker build, and live SABnzbd validation.

The current review-response head changes the history-window control from fixed string presets to Homarr's existing numeric option, defaults it to 7 days, and simplifies the archived-history conditional. The guarded compare against the reviewed parent shows only the intended Downloads/SABnzbd code, tests, API/request typing, and documentation files.

Hosted GitHub Actions for the current fork-based head still require maintainer approval before they can run, so fresh CI for this review-response commit is pending.

## Notes

This redesign follows maintainer feedback to keep the feature in the Downloads widget and reuse Homarr's existing option, translation, request-handler, and integration patterns.

title: feat: Windows-style board switcher overlay (Alt-Tab style) when cycling boards
body:
## Summary

Add a Windows-style application-switcher overlay (Alt-Tab style) that appears while cycling between boards with the keyboard, making it easy to see and pick between boards at a glance.

## Motivation

This was suggested by @Meierschlumpf in a comment on the board keyboard shortcuts PR:

> [PR #6393 comment](https://github.com/homarr-labs/homarr/pull/6393#issuecomment-5012330605): _Something like this, just for the boards_ — showing a Windows-style switcher UI screenshot.

![Windows-style switcher example](https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/1d6e8728-76da-495a-885f-9619ed93e3de)

This builds naturally on top of the board-switching keyboard shortcuts (next/previous + mod+shift+1-9) that land in #6393. Instead of instantly jumping boards, the shortcut could hold a preview overlay with board cards (logo + name), highlight the selected one, and switch only when the modifier keys are released.

## Proposed behavior

- Press and hold MOD + SHIFT + left/right arrow (or a number) to open an overlay showing all boards as cards (logo + name), similar to the OS app switcher.
- The currently selected board is highlighted.
- Keep pressing arrows/numbers to change the selection.
- Release the modifier keys to switch to the selected board.
- Escape dismisses without switching.

## Reference implementation

An exploratory implementation was drafted and then removed from #6393 to keep that PR minimal. It includes:
- Overlay UI using Mantine Portal + board cards (Avatar logo, name, Kbd number badge), selection highlight, scrollIntoView, Escape to dismiss, modifier-release to commit
- A pure getNextBoardIndex wraparound helper and unit tests

This should be reconstructed/reworked here rather than folded into the hotkeys PR.

## Acceptance criteria

- Overlay renders above the board content (fixed positioning, high z-index)
- Board cards show logo and name, and are keyboard-navigable
- Selection commits on modifier-key release; Escape cancels
- Works for users with and without board change access
- Covered by unit tests for the navigation logic
- Documentation updated in apps/docs/docs/advanced/keyboard-shortcuts/index.mdx

title: feat(boards): allow addItem to target a specific section
body:
## Description

The `board.addItem` endpoint (OpenAPI `POST /api/boards/items` and MCP tool `board_addItem`) always places new items in the first **empty** section of a board. For boards organised into named **category** sections there is no API-reachable way to add an item to a specific category: `addItem` can't target one, and `saveBoard` (which can reposition items) is not exposed via OpenAPI or MCP. The only workaround is editing the database directly.

This PR adds:

- an optional `sectionId` to `addItemToBoardSchema`. When provided, the item is placed at the next free grid position of that section (the existing placement algorithm, unchanged — just pointed at the given section). Only `empty` and `category` sections are allowed; a `dynamic` section id is rejected with `BAD_REQUEST`, and an unknown id with `NOT_FOUND`. When omitted, behaviour is exactly as before (first empty section), so existing OpenAPI/MCP clients are unaffected.
- the sections of each board (`id`, `kind`, `name`, position) in the `getAllBoards` response, so API/MCP clients can discover the `sectionId` to pass without an additional tool (per review feedback, instead of a separate `getSections` procedure).
- tests (default placement, section-targeted placement, unknown section, dynamic section, empty section id, section listing in `getAllBoards`).

Motivation: automation and agent clients (e.g. via the built-in MCP server) managing a categorised dashboard — "add an app tile for service X in the *Local Apps* category".

Verified locally: `pnpm typecheck` (all 37 packages) and the board router test suite (51 tests, including 6 new) pass; changed files formatted with `oxfmt`.

title: feat: Expand Homarr API Coverage to Support Full Dashboard Automation
body:
### Describe the feature you'd like to request

### Summary

Homarr’s current API (https://homarr.dev/docs/management/api/) is too limited to fully automate dashboard creation and configuration. Critical GUI‑only actions—such as creating search engines, adding dashboards, configuring widgets, and managing admin users, not all can be reproduced programmatically. This prevents reliable infrastructure‑as‑code workflows (e.g., Ansible playbooks) and forces users to manually rebuild dashboards through the GUI.

This feature request proposes expanding the API to cover all GUI interactions, enabling complete automation and reproducible deployments.

I know we can make a backup but it contains a sqlite db and a text, nothing that can be use to be easily edited and avoid to do everything in the gui...

###Problem Description

I am building an Ansible playbook to automate Homarr deployment and configuration. The goal is to redeploy or rebuild my dashboard simply by applying a playbook and feeding a text file containing the desired configuration.

However, the current API only supports a small subset of actions. Many essential operations are GUI‑only, including:

    Creating search engines

    Creating additional dashboards

    Adding, removing, or configuring widgets

    Managing dashboard layout

    Managing categories

    Managing services

    Managing admin users

    Exporting/importing dashboard configuration

    Setting global settings (theme, language, etc.)

Additionally, the API currently requires an existing admin user to generate an API key. This creates a bootstrap problem:

    I can automate user creation, but only normal users.

    I cannot automate creation of the initial admin user, because generating the API key requires logging into the GUI as the admin.

    Therefore, full automation is impossible.

### Requested Features

**1. API Endpoint: Create Admin User**

Allow creation of an admin user via API, including:

    Role assignment

    Password definition

    Ability to generate an API key without GUI login

This solves the bootstrap problem and enables fully automated deployments.

**2. API Endpoint: Create Search Engines**

Expose CRUD operations for search engines:

    Create search engine

    Update search engine

    Delete search engine

    List search engines

Fields should match the GUI:

    Name

    URL template

    Icon

    Category

    Default status

**3. API Endpoint: Create & Manage Dashboards**

Expose full dashboard management:

    Create dashboard

    Delete dashboard

    Rename dashboard

    Set default dashboard

    Export dashboard configuration

    Import dashboard configuration

**4. API Endpoint: Manage Widgets**

Expose CRUD operations for widgets:

    Add widget

    Remove widget

    Configure widget settings

    Move widget on the grid

    Resize widget

Widget types should be fully supported:

    Apps

    Search bar

    Weather

    Calendar

    Custom widgets

    Etc.

**5. API Endpoint: Manage Services**

Expose CRUD operations for services:

    Add service

    Remove service

    Configure service fields

    Assign service to dashboard

**6. API Endpoint: Global Settings**

Expose configuration for:

    Theme

    Language

    Layout

    Custom CSS

    Global search settings

    Backup/restore

**7. API Endpoint: Full Configuration Export/Import**

Provide a single JSON/YAML export containing:

    Dashboards

    Widgets

    Search engines

    Services

    Categories

    Global settings

And a matching import endpoint.

This would allow:

    Infrastructure‑as‑code

    Git‑versioned dashboard definitions

    Instant redeployment

Why This Matters

Homarr is positioned as a modern, customizable dashboard. But without a complete API, it cannot be reliably automated or integrated into DevOps workflows.

Adding these endpoints would enable:

    Ansible automation

    Terraform modules (or Open Tofu)

    GitOps workflows

    CI/CD deployment of dashboards

    Backup/restore without GUI

    Multi‑environment reproducibility

This dramatically increases Homarr’s value for power users and self‑hosters.
Proposed Minimal Viable Implementation

If full coverage is too large for one release, the following subset would already unlock automation:

    Create admin user via API

    Generate API key via API

    Create dashboard

    Create search engine

    Export/import dashboard configuration

This alone would allow complete reproducible deployments.

**8.a API Endpoint: Generate a backup**

Homarr’s backup feature is currently GUI‑only and produces a SQLite database file. For automation (e.g., Ansible), an API endpoint is needed to trigger backups without manual interaction.
Requested behavior

Provide an API endpoint that can generate a backup in one or both formats:

    SQLite backup  
    Same as the GUI.
    Endpoint example: POST /backup/sqlite  
    Returns the raw .db file as binary.

    JSON/YAML backup  
    Structured export of all configuration (dashboards, widgets, search engines, services, settings).
    Endpoint example: POST /backup/export  
    Returns a full config object suitable for GitOps and IaC.

Both formats serve different automation needs, and either one would already improve reproducibility.

**8.b API Endpoint: Restore a backup**

To complement the backup endpoint, Homarr should provide a simple restore mechanism through the API. This allows full automation of redeployment without touching the GUI.
Requested behavior

Support restoring from either backup format:

    SQLite restore  
    Endpoint example: POST /restore/sqlite  
    Accepts the same .db file produced by the GUI or /backup/sqlite.

    JSON/YAML restore  
    Endpoint example: POST /restore/import  
    Accepts a structured configuration export and rebuilds dashboards, widgets, search engines, services, and settings.

Both restore methods enable fully automated Homarr provisioning and disaster recovery.

### Conclusion

Homarr’s GUI is excellent, but the lack of API coverage prevents automation. Expanding the API to cover all GUI interactions would make Homarr dramatically more powerful and suitable for modern DevOps workflows.

I would be happy to help test or provide example Ansible playbooks once these endpoints exist.
I had started one but I had to make it much more robust by querying the actual existing dashboard ids, etc...

title: fix(docker): report container CPU as a total-system percentage
body:
This branch started as the Unraid CPU fix for #6082. That landed separately in #6510 on 2026-08-22, so the Unraid hunk is gone and what is left is a different fix on a different file. Retitling rather than opening a new PR, so the review history stays attached.

## Problem

`calculateCpuUsage` in `packages/request-handler/src/docker.ts` divides the container's cumulative `total_usage` by the cumulative `system_cpu_usage`. Both counters run from container start, so the result is the container's lifetime average, not what it is doing now. A container that was busy an hour ago keeps reporting a high number long after the load ended.

It then multiplies by `online_cpus`, following docker stats' per-core convention, where 134% means 1.34 busy cores. Every other CPU reading in Homarr is a 0-100% share of the machine, so the same dashboard shows two different scales.

## Fix

Compare the latest reading against the previous one, which is what `precpu_stats` is for, and report the plain ratio. `system_cpu_usage` already accumulates across all cores, so the ratio is the whole-machine share and cannot exceed 100%.

`precpu_stats` is absent when stats are fetched in one-shot mode, Podman being the case that matters here, so the deltas fall back to the cumulative totals and behave as before rather than dividing by zero.

## The part worth a second opinion

Dropping the `online_cpus` multiplier changes what the number means: a container using 1.34 cores on an 8 core host reported 134% before and reports about 17% now. I think matching the rest of Homarr's 0-100% scale is the right call, but it is a visible change and it is yours to make. Say so if you would rather keep docker stats' convention and I will restore the multiplier while keeping the delta fix.

## Tests

`docker.spec.ts` covers the delta calculation, the fallback when `precpu_stats` is missing, and that several fully busy cores stay at or below 100%. The two existing expectations that encoded the old per-core scale were updated with the arithmetic spelled out.

title: fix(integrations): support UniFi controller default ports
body:
## Summary

Fixes the misleading TLS error produced when a UniFi integration URL omits its port.

`node-unifi` always connects over HTTPS. UniFi OS consoles such as UDR and UDM normally use port 443, while self-hosted UniFi Network controllers normally use 8443. Homarr now:

- preserves an explicitly supplied port
- tries port 443 first when no port is supplied
- falls back to 8443 only after a connection or controller-detection failure
- does not hide authentication failures by retrying another port

title: feat(app): support path-only hrefs for multi-hostname access
body:
**This is a minimal alternative to #5595.**

Claude's description follows.
----
## Summary

Allow app card hrefs to be **path-only** (e.g. `/cockpit/`) in addition to
absolute URLs. A path-only href is rendered as a plain `<a href="/cockpit/">` and
resolved by the browser against the current origin, so a single dashboard works
across every hostname the device answers on (mDNS `.local`, a VPN FQDN, a
DHCP-provided FQDN) without baking a hostname into each card at registration time.

This is the motivating case for self-hosted / reverse-proxy setups where the same
Homarr instance is reached over more than one hostname and SSO/cookies/redirects
are already per-host.

## Scope

Deliberately narrow — just the app-card surface:

- `packages/validation` — `appHrefSchema` accepts absolute URL **or** path-only form
- `packages/common` — `resolveServerUrl(app)` centralises the
  pingUrl-or-absolute-or-null resolution used server-side
- `packages/widgets` — app card, ping indicator, and bookmarks sub-label handle
  path-only entries
- `packages/api` — the ping router routes through `resolveServerUrl`

No changes to the integration framework. Path-only support for integration
`externalUrl` (the `RenderablePath` work) and the URL-typing refactor from #5595
are intentionally left out so this can be reviewed and merged on its own; they can
follow as a separate PR.

## Server-side resolution

Path-only hrefs resolve to `null` server-side. The server has no canonical
hostname for a path-only app and must not synthesize one from request headers
(that would be a header-spoofing / SSRF vector). In the ping widget, a path-only
href without an explicit `pingUrl` returns a `CONFLICT` and the indicator shows an
indeterminate state rather than up/down. Apps that need server-side ping coverage
under a multi-hostname deployment set an explicit `pingUrl`.

## Backward compatibility

Additive. Absolute hrefs behave exactly as before — `resolveServerUrl` returns
them unchanged, the ping widget and bookmarks render identically, and no existing
app or integration changes behaviour. The only new acceptance is the path-only
form.

## Validation

The path-only branch rejects `javascript:`, protocol-relative `//host/...`,
single-slash root `/`, consecutive slashes mid-path, backslashes, whitespace,
C0/C1 control characters, and Unicode zero-width / bidi / formatting characters
(display-spoofing protection). Absolute-URL validation is unchanged.

## Documentation

`apps/docs/docs/management/apps/index.mdx` — documents the path-only URL form on
the App URL field, and notes that the status check needs an explicit Ping URL for
path-only apps.

## Testing

- `resolveServerUrl`: pingUrl precedence, absolute pass-through, path-only → null,
  null inputs, path-only-with-pingUrl
- `appHrefSchema`: accepts absolute and path-only; rejects the cases above
- Bookmarks sub-label: renders the path for path-only entries, hostname for
  absolute

----

body:
Bumps the npm_and_yarn group with 2 updates in the / directory: [esbuild](https://github.com/evanw/esbuild) and [undici](https://github.com/nodejs/undici). Updates `esbuild` from 0.25.12 to 0.28.1
Release notes

Sourced from esbuild's releases.

v0.28.1

  • Disallow \ in local development server HTTP requests (GHSA-g7r4-m6w7-qqqr)

    This release fixes a security issue where HTTP requests to esbuild's local development server could traverse outside of the serve directory on Windows using a \ backslash character. It happened due to the use of Go's path.Clean() function, which only handles Unix-style / characters. HTTP requests with paths containing \ are no longer allowed.

    Thanks to @​dellalibera for reporting this issue.

  • Add integrity checks to the Deno API (GHSA-gv7w-rqvm-qjhr)

    The previous release of esbuild added integrity checks to esbuild's npm install script. This release also adds integrity checks to esbuild's Deno install script. Now esbuild's Deno API will also fail with an error if the downloaded esbuild binary contains something other than the expected content.

    Note that esbuild's Deno API installs from registry.npmjs.org by default, but allows the NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY environment variable to override this with a custom package registry. This change means that the esbuild executable served by NPM_CONFIG_REGISTRY must now match the expected content.

    Thanks to @​sondt99 for reporting this issue.

  • Avoid inlining using and await using declarations (#4482)

    Previously esbuild's minifier sometimes incorrectly inlined using and await using declarations into subsequent uses of that declaration, which then fails to dispose of the resource correctly. This bug happened because inlining was done for let and const declarations by avoiding doing it for var declarations, which no longer worked when more declaration types were added. Here's an example:

    // Original code
{
  using x = new Resource()
  x.activate()
}

    // Old output (with --minify)
    
new Resource().activate();
    

    // New output (with --minify)
    
{using e=new Resource;e.activate()}

  • Fix module evaluation when an error is thrown (#4461, #4467)

    If an error is thrown during module evaluation, esbuild previously didn't preserve the state of the module for subsequent module references. This was observable if import() or require() is used to import a module multiple times. The thrown error is supposed to be thrown by every call to import() or require(), not just the first. With this release, esbuild will now throw the same error every time you call import() or require() on a module that throws during its evaluation.

  • Fix some edge cases around the new operator (#4477)

    Previously esbuild incorrectly printed certain edge cases involving complex expressions inside the target of a new expression (specifically an optional chain and/or a tagged template literal). The generated code for the new target was not correctly wrapped with parentheses, and either contained a syntax error or had different semantics. These edge cases have been fixed so that they now correctly wrap the new target in parentheses. Here is an example of some affected code:

    // Original code
new (foo()`bar`)()
new (foo()?.bar)()

    // Old output
    
new foo()bar();
    
new (foo())?.bar();

... (truncated)

Changelog

Sourced from esbuild's changelog.

Changelog: 2025

This changelog documents all esbuild versions published in the year 2025 (versions 0.25.0 through 0.27.2).

0.27.2

  • Allow import path specifiers starting with #/ (#4361)

    Previously the specification for package.json disallowed import path specifiers starting with #/, but this restriction has recently been relaxed and support for it is being added across the JavaScript ecosystem. One use case is using it for a wildcard pattern such as mapping #/* to ./src/* (previously you had to use another character such as #_* instead, which was more confusing). There is some more context in nodejs/node#49182.

    This change was contributed by @​hybrist.

  • Automatically add the -webkit-mask prefix (#4357, #4358)

    This release automatically adds the -webkit- vendor prefix for the mask CSS shorthand property:

    /* Original code */
main {
  mask: url(x.png) center/5rem no-repeat
}

    /* Old output (with --target=chrome110) */
    
main {
    
mask: url(x.png) center/5rem no-repeat;
    
}
    

    /* New output (with --target=chrome110) */
    
main {
    
-webkit-mask: url(x.png) center/5rem no-repeat;
    
mask: url(x.png) center/5rem no-repeat;
    
}

    This change was contributed by @​BPJEnnova.

  • Additional minification of switch statements (#4176, #4359)

    This release contains additional minification patterns for reducing switch statements. Here is an example:

    // Original code
switch (x) {
  case 0:
    foo()
    break
  case 1:
  default:
    bar()
}

title: feat: Support Kubernetes integration as dashboard widgets instead of a global tool for multi-tenant access control
body:
### Describe the feature you'd like to request

Currently, in Homarr v1.x, the Kubernetes integration functions exclusively as a global monolithic screen located under "Tools -> Kubernetes". While it provides a great overview, it lacks flexibility. There is no way to display specific Kubernetes metrics directly on standard dashboards. 

Furthermore, because it is a global tool, we cannot safely isolate cluster data when managing multiple environments for different teams or external vendors. Anyone with access to the Tools menu can see all connected clusters and all their details.


We need the ability to decouple the Kubernetes integration from being just a global tool and transform it into a flexible, customizable **Dashboard Widget**. 

When adding this Kubernetes widget to a board, an administrator should be able to configure exactly **which specific cluster data** they want to extract and display. 

The widget settings should include:
1. **Cluster Selector:** Choose which configured cluster/context to pull data from.
2. **Data Type / Metric Selector:** A granular way to choose what exactly this specific widget instance will show on the panel. For example, checkboxes or a dropdown to display *only*:
   * **Hardware Capacity only:** Just the CPU/Memory progress circles.
   * **Specific Resource Counter only:** For instance, a small card showing only the number of active Pods, or only the number of Ingresses.
   * **Status lists:** A simple list of failed/restarting workloads for that specific cluster.

This granular selector allows us to build clean, customized welcome dashboards for different projects or vendors. For example, on Vendor A's board, I can place a widget showing *only* their cluster's Pod count and CPU usage, without giving them access to the global tool or exposing other sensitive cluster details (like Secrets, Nodes, or other clusters).

### Additional information

This would massively improve Homarr's usability for multi-tenant and enterprise-like DevOps environments where different teams or external vendors share the same dashboard instance but manage different infrastructure parts. Transforming the Kubernetes integration into customizable widgets balances infrastructure transparency with strict "need-to-know" security boundaries.

body:
### Describe the bug

We use Jumpcloud as an OIDC authentication provider, and connect only one group per user for OIDC authentication. In this case, the list of groups is sent as a string (just the one group name), not an array. Homarr seems to expect an array, and group assignment is not working in such case.

In the debug output we see (abbreviated):
E.g. with single group - group assignment not working:
```
  "email": "test.user@example.com",
  "groups": "homarr-user-group",
```

E.g. with multiple groups - group assignment working:
```
  "email": "test.user@example.com",
  "groups": [
    "homarr-user-group",
    "homarr-dummy-group"
  ],
```


### Steps to reproduce

* Configure Homarr OAuth with a provider that sends a sinlge OAuth groups as a string instead of an array
* Create group with same name in Homarr
* Map permissions to that group
* Log in with user mapped to that single group
* Observe user being created, but not mapped to that group in Homarr

### Impact

Impact: medium I'd say - it's a bit tedious to debug because it's not obvious what's going on, and only from the debug logs one might be able to deduce the correlation of the single group not being in an array might cause the group mapping problem

Workaround: ensure to always send at least two groups

### Additional information

I found a similar bug in the harbor registry (https://goharbor.io/) that led me to figure out this issue.

Helm
